descriptor: The largest animal known to have ever lived, sustained almost entirely by tiny shrimp-like krill.

range.summary: All the major oceans, from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters, with resident groups off Sri Lanka and in the Gulf of California.

population.unit: Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia) in the Southern Ocean

source.label: Branch et al. 2004, Marine Mammal Science; Branch 2007, IDCR/SOWER circumpolar surveys

population.note: The 1904 and 1973 values are model back-estimates of the pre-whaling and lowest populations; later points are survey estimates south of 60°S. Worldwide, IUCN estimates 5,000 to 15,000 mature blue whales.

threats.title: Ship strikes
threats.detail: Collisions in busy shipping lanes off California and Sri Lanka kill whales every year.

threats.title: Ocean noise
threats.detail: Shipping and seismic surveys mask the low calls blue whales use to find each other.

threats.title: Entanglement
threats.detail: Fishing gear and lines can wrap around whales and wound or drown them.

threats.title: Shifting krill supply
threats.detail: Warming seas and krill fishing could reduce the swarms the whales need to feed.

places.name: Mirissa
places.note: Blue whales feed a few kilometres offshore, close to a busy shipping lane.

places.name: Santa Barbara Channel
places.note: A major summer feeding ground for eastern North Pacific blue whales.

places.name: Loreto, Gulf of California
places.note: Mothers and calves in calm water inside a marine national park.

places.name: Les Escoumins, St. Lawrence Estuary
places.note: North Atlantic blue whales feed on krill, sometimes seen from shore.

sightings.tip: Seasons depend on the site: December to April off Sri Lanka, February to April in the Gulf of California, and July to September off California and in the St. Lawrence.

actions.title: Back slower shipping
actions.detail: Voluntary speed limits in whale zones cut fatal strikes and also reduce underwater noise.

actions.title: Watch whales responsibly
actions.detail: Choose operators that keep their distance and never chase or cut off a whale.

actions.title: Skip krill-oil supplements
actions.detail: Antarctic krill is the main food of recovering blue whales, so plant-based omega-3 is the safer choice.

actions.title: Report sightings
actions.detail: Logging sightings in citizen science apps helps map where ships and whales overlap.
